summary:
Wasl (Arabic for "connected") is a free web app that finds the best day to land at the lunar south pole. There, the Sun stays near the horizon, so one ridge can cut a lander's solar power or hide Earth and break its radio link.

Pick one of 12 sites (NASA Artemis III candidate regions and real landing sites) or tap any point near the pole. Wasl simulates a 14-day mission hour by hour for every landing day of the year. It uses real NASA LRO LOLA terrain to compute the skyline around the site, and Sun and Earth positions computed in the browser. It then names the best, typical and worst landing day.

Users can live the mission in a cockpit with battery, alarms and countdowns, read a survival report, and explore the real terrain in 3D, in English or Arabic, on any phone.

Our Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons within 0.002°, and our terrain results correlate at 0.98 with NASA's 18.6-year illumination map.

Working prototype; limits: 240 m terrain, no thermal model, illustrative lander power.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Wasl finds the best day to land at a lunar south-pole site so the lander keeps both sunlight and contact with Earth. It has three parts:

1. Plan: a year calendar where every day is coloured by how much of a 14-day mission has Sun and Earth together. One tap gives the best, typical and worst landing day, with sunlight %, Earth-in-view %, longest darkness, first sunset, a side-by-side site comparison and a CSV download. Buttons open JPL Horizons for the same place and time so anyone can check the numbers.

2. Live it: a cockpit that plays the mission minute by minute: the real terrain skyline, the Sun and Earth in their true positions, battery, solar power, Earth link, alarms and countdowns.

3. 3D: 48 km of real LOLA terrain around the site, lit by the Sun at its computed position.

How it works: from NASA's LRO LOLA south-pole elevation model (LDEM_75S_240M, 240 m per pixel) we compute the highest terrain angle in every direction (every 0.25°) out to 200 km. For every hour, the browser computes where the Sun and Earth are in the lander's sky (Astronomy Engine, IAU Moon rotation model). We check how much of the Sun is above the skyline (power) and whether Earth is above it (radio link), and run a battery model with a 20% reserve. This is repeated for every landing day of the year.

Validation: our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.002°, and our horizons correlate at r = 0.98 with NASA's LOLA 18.6-year illumination map (40 points south of 85°S).

What benefits does it have?

It answers in seconds a question that normally needs terrain models, ephemerides and power budgets combined by hand. It is free, needs no install, works on phones, and every number can be checked against NASA tools.

What is the intended impact?

Mission planners get a fast first screen of sites and landing days before detailed analysis. Students and the public, including Arabic speakers, can see why the south pole is hard and follow Artemis and commercial Moon landings.

What tools did you use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step), three.js for 3D, Astronomy Engine for Sun and Earth positions, Web Audio for sound, Python for terrain preprocessing and validation, GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/Mahmoud-Magdy-ai/wasl8-lunar (MIT licence)

How is your project creative?

Most tools show terrain, images or sky positions separately. Wasl combines them into one decision (which day to land) and then lets you live that day from inside the lander, so the numbers become an experience anyone can understand.

What factors did your team consider?

Accuracy (validated against two NASA references), honesty about limits, access (free, phones, English and Arabic) and traceability (every number links to a NASA source). Limits we state openly: 240 m terrain smooths small hills; no thermal model; Earth visibility is line of sight only; lander power numbers are illustrative. Status: working prototype, running today at the live link.
